newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin op looks imminent, security tightened.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin op looks imminent, security tightened.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's long-awaited heart operation looked imminent on Tuesday as the Kremlin sealed off the hospital where a team of Russian specialists will carry out bypass surgery.

Extra police kept TV crews and photographers well away from the Cardiological Centre in Moscow's western suburbs and one private radio station, Ekho Moskvy, said it had confirmed the operation would take place on Tuesday.

It was unclear if Yeltsin had already been moved to the hospital. Officially the Kremlin would say only that the operation to improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's ailing heart could take place "in the next few days".

This was the laconic formula used in a communique issued after a meeting of doctors, including renowned U.S. surgeon Michael DeBakey, on Monday at the Barvikha sanatorium where Yeltsin, 65, has been preparing for surgery.

If the operation, led by Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin, takes place as expected on Tuesday it will coincide with trade union strikes and protests in Moscow and elsewhere across Russia against delayed wages.
It will also coincide with the U.S. presidential election, which will take the world news spotlight away from Moscow for at least 24 hours.

Yeltsin's long illness, which has removed him from the political front line since just before his victory in last July's presidential election, has encouraged Kremlin infighting and uncertainty over who is making decisions.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, standing in for Yeltsin, has been trying to project an atmosphere of business as usual but uncertainty has been stimulated by the Kremlin's secrecy over the timing and details of Yeltsin's operation.
By the standards of the Soviet Union, Moscow has shown unprecedented candour but by Western standards has released very little medical information.

Monday's bulletin said Yeltsin's blood pressure, temperature and pulse were normal but gave no other details except to say his current condition showed "all organs and systems to be functioning at an optimal level".
"This makes it possible to undertake the operation with a high level of certainty and confidence," the doctors said.

Yeltsin is expected to sign a decree shortly before the operation handing over to Chernomyrdin his control over Russia's nuclear deterrent. If all goes well in the operation, expected to last between six and eight hours, he will take back his powers soon after he recovers consciousness.

There were other signs the operation on the 65-year-old president, first announced in September, was imminent, among them the postponement of a visit by Defence Minister Igor Rodionov to Russia's Northern Fleet on Tuesday.
There was no mention of Yeltsin's operation. But it would be highly unusual for the defence minister to be away from the capital while Yeltsin, who is commander-in-chief, undergoes surgery.
The head of the Russian Orthodox Church offered prayers for Yeltsin in the Kazan cathedral on Red Square.

"Heal the illnesses, the spiritual and corporeal ailments of the president of our Russian land, forgive him his transgressions, witting and unwitting, deliver him soon from his sickbed and restore him to good health," Patriarch Alexiy said.
Financial markets are watching the medical bulletins closely, though they are more worried by the fundamentals of Russia's economy.
Dealers say a successful operation which allows Yeltsin to return to work could point to stability in Russia and increase chances of an investment boom.
